response.summary: The paper proposes MASE, a minimax notion for average coalition-deviation gain, together with treewidth-based hardness and an FTPL/dynamic-programming algorithm. The direction is interesting, but central hardness and convergence arguments contain substantial gaps, and the empirical evidence is too limited and internally inconsistent to compensate.
strengths: The minimax relaxation gives an always-existing, clearly defined objective for coalition deviations and explicitly states its transferable-utility interpretation (pp. 3–4).
The utility-dependency graph and tree-decomposition dynamic program are potentially useful structural ideas, and the Carathéodory argument suggests sparse representations (pp. 5–7, 16–17).
The experiments examine unilateral robustness, coalition robustness, and welfare rather than reporting only the optimized objective (pp. 8–10, 26–29).
weaknesses: The deviator-side FTPL proof appears invalid: the perturbation in Eq. G.1 is shared across coalitions and supplies no coalition-specific randomization, yet the analysis treats selection of S as a perturbed extra root decision. Deterministic switching among coalitions can incur linear regret. The stated probability bound also contains the impossible expression 1−exp(2η|T|)<0 (pp. 25–26). This undermines Theorems 5.3–5.4 and the main algorithmic guarantee.

The hardness proofs are not rigorous as written. Theorem 4.1's construction uses negative utilities despite the assumed [0,1] range and simply asserts, without establishing, that an optimum places half its mass on each all-equal bit profile (p. 15). The treewidth reduction reasons largely through attained utility rather than the deviation-gain objective and does not cleanly prove the claimed equivalence (p. 16).

The evidence is narrow and inconsistent. In Prisoner's Dilemma, the stated MASE mixture has unilateral deviation gain 0.1, so its coalition exploitability is at least 0.1, but the purported LP ground truth in Figure 2 is plotted near zero while the learned MASE is near 0.1 (pp. 8–9). Larger experiments use random polymatrix games without reporting actual treewidth, and runtime remains linear in |S|, which is exponential when all coalitions are included (pp. 8, 29–32).
response.score_rationale: Although the concept and treewidth-based approach are promising, the missing coalition perturbation is a central technical failure in the claimed matching algorithm, while the lower-bound proofs and experiments have additional unresolved problems. Major new analysis would be required, warranting rejection rather than a marginal score.

response.summary: The paper proposes MASE, a minimax coalition-deviation objective, and relates its computation to the treewidth of a utility-dependency graph. The direction is interesting, but central upper-bound guarantees are not established by the supplied proofs, and the empirical evaluation is too limited to compensate.
strengths: The always-defined minimax formulation provides a clear alternative when strong equilibria do not exist (pp. 3–4).
The utility-dependency graph and tree-decomposition dynamic-programming perspective are potentially useful structural tools (pp. 4–8).
The paper attempts a broad package of hardness, representation, algorithms, and empirical illustrations, with several proofs included in the appendices.
weaknesses: The deviator regret analysis is incomplete/inconsistent: the implemented perturbation is not clearly indexed by coalition, selecting among coalitions would require an additional perturbation/complexity term, and the claimed stability bound even contains the impossible inequality Pr(change) ≤ 1−exp(2η|T|) (pp. 25–26). Thus Theorems 5.3–5.4 and the main runtime guarantee are unsupported.

The correlator stability proof factorizes conditional probabilities across bags even though conditioning on the root/parent decisions, which themselves depend on subtree messages, can couple these events (pp. 21–23). No valid independence argument is supplied, undermining Theorem 5.2.

Several other claims are overstated or insufficiently justified: the NP-hardness reduction violates the stated [0,1] utility range and gives only a terse, unclear equivalence argument (p. 15); Lemma 6.1 does not show equivalence of all optimizers; and experiments are mainly tiny games or random polymatrix instances with coalitions of size at most two (pp. 8–10, 27–32).
response.score_rationale: The formulation and treewidth approach have promise, but the missing coalition perturbation and questionable stability arguments affect the central matching algorithm rather than peripheral details. With only limited empirical evidence and additional proof gaps, substantial revision is needed before the main claims can be trusted.

response.summary: The paper proposes MASE, a minimax notion based on average coalition-deviation gain, and seeks matching treewidth-dependent hardness and algorithms. The direction is interesting, but central correctness gaps in the online-learning algorithm and reductions prevent the main claims from being established.
strengths: The coalition-deviation objective is clearly defined and always admits an optimizer, while its distinction from strong Nash equilibrium is acknowledged (pp. 3–4).
The utility-dependency graph and tree-decomposition dynamic-programming perspective are potentially useful structural ideas (pp. 4–7).
The appendices provide extensive attempted proofs and experiments across canonical and random polymatrix games (pp. 14–33).
weaknesses: The deviator FTPL argument appears invalid: its perturbation has no coalition-indexed component, yet the proof treats coalition selection as a perturbed root action; the claimed stability inequality even contains the impossible bound 1−exp(2η|T|)<0 (pp. 25–26). Thus Theorems 5.3–5.4 are unsupported.

The complexity claims contain major inconsistencies. The algorithm executes T updates but is reported as taking only O(√T·|S||T|A^{tw+1}) time (p. 8), and the NP-hardness construction uses utilities −ui despite assuming Ui∈[0,1] (pp. 2, 15). The leap from an exponential LP to NP-completeness is also not justified (p. 4).

Evidence is limited mainly to tiny canonical games and synthetic polymatrix instances, with no strong structured-game benchmark. Several presentation/proof errors further reduce confidence, including reversed min/max notation in the meta-game (p. 5) and the false assertion |N(i)|≤tw(G) rather than at most tw(G)+1 (p. 17).
response.score_rationale: Although the proposed objective and treewidth viewpoint have some novelty, the missing coalition perturbation and invalid stability proof undermine the main upper bound, while the hardness and runtime statements also have substantive gaps. These are central rather than easily localized issues, warranting rejection.

response.summary: The paper proposes MASE, a minimax notion based on coalitions’ average gain from fixed joint deviations, and relates its computation to the treewidth of a utility-dependency graph. The direction is interesting, but central hardness and algorithmic proofs contain substantial errors, so the main claimed complexity characterization is not established.
strengths: The objective is clearly motivated as an always-existing alternative to strong equilibrium, with a useful transferable-utility interpretation (pp. 3–4).
The utility-dependency graph and tree-decomposition dynamic-programming perspective are potentially valuable for succinct games (pp. 4–7).
The paper includes LP comparisons, several illustrative games, random polymatrix experiments, and runtime measurements (pp. 8–10, 26–31).
weaknesses: The NP-hardness proof constructs utilities taking values −ui despite defining all utilities in [0,1], and the asserted characterization of the optimal bit distribution is not adequately derived (p. 15). The fixed-parameter proof then analyzes average utilities rather than the MASE deviation-gain objective, leaving its key equivalence unsupported as written (p. 16).

The deviator regret proof is invalid as presented: its perturbation has no coalition-specific component, yet it treats coalition selection as an independently perturbed root decision; coalition switches therefore are not controlled by the stated stability argument. It also gives the impossible bound 1−exp(2η|T|), which is negative (pp. 25–26). This undermines Theorems 5.3–5.4 and the main runtime guarantee.

The concept only tests unconditional fixed coalition deviations and averages transferable gains, so its relationship to standard strong/correlated coalition equilibrium is narrower than the framing suggests. Empirical evidence is mostly small canonical games or random instances and does not compensate for the theoretical gaps (pp. 8–10, 27–31).
response.score_rationale: The proposed concept and treewidth-based approach are promising, but errors in both principal lower-bound proofs and the deviator’s regret analysis affect the paper’s core theorems rather than peripheral details. Major new proofs and likely algorithmic modifications are required; hence reject.

response.summary: The paper proposes MASE, a minimax average coalition-deviation criterion, and attempts to characterize its complexity through a utility-dependency graph and treewidth. The direction is potentially interesting, but central proofs supporting both the claimed algorithm and hardness results contain substantial errors, while the experiments provide limited validation.
strengths: MASE is a clear, always-existing relaxation of strong equilibrium, with an intuitive LP formulation and interpretation under transferable coalition utility (pp. 3–4, 14–15).
Relating computation to a utility-dependency graph and using dynamic programming over a tree decomposition is a promising structural approach (pp. 4–7).
The paper includes explicit appendices and compares unilateral versus coalition exploitability on several illustrative games (pp. 26–29).
weaknesses: The main convergence theorem is not established. In the deviator analysis, the claimed probability upper bound is 1−exp(2η|T|), which is negative, and the implementation supplies no coalition-indexed perturbation that would justify stability when the selected coalition changes (pp. 25–26). This invalidates Theorems 5.3–5.4 and thus the principal upper bound.

The hardness proofs have serious gaps. Theorem 4.1 constructs negative utilities despite the assumed [0,1] range and makes insufficiently justified claims about the optimal distribution (p. 15). Theorem 4.3's written argument analyzes average utility rather than the defined deviation gain, so its stated equivalence and sampling conclusion do not follow as presented (p. 16).

The tractability and empirical claims are overstated: runtime is linear in |S|, which is exponential when all coalitions are allowed, as in the motivating setting (pp. 8, 10, 25). Experiments are mostly small canonical games or random polymatrix instances restricted to coalitions of size at most two, and compare against algorithms not designed for the same objective (pp. 8–10, 26–32).
response.score_rationale: The concept and treewidth-based direction have merit, but the invalid deviator regret proof undermines the main algorithmic contribution, and the hardness arguments are not rigorous as written. These are central rather than cosmetic issues, warranting rejection despite the promising framing.
